issues.line_text: I'd done this before on other investigations. Worked until dawn, gotten so deep in the hunt that I'd write feverishly for hours. Found pages of notes later that barely made sense, written in that late-night clarity that dissolves by morning.
issues.description: Josh claiming he's done 'other investigations' before implies a history of investigative work that doesn't exist. Josh is a podcaster/writer who's only been doing this for 4 years (per his email from Derek). More critically, this inadvertently hints at a pattern of fugue-state behavior (writing he doesn't remember clearly) that he's normalizing. The phrase 'pages of notes later that barely made sense' is too close to dissociative behavior.
issues.fix: I'd done this before on other stories. Worked until dawn, gotten so deep in the research that I'd write feverishly for hours. Found pages of notes later that seemed overwrought, written in that late-night intensity that feels profound at 3 AM but melodramatic by morning.
issues.rationale: Changes 'investigations' to 'stories' (fits his writer persona), changes 'barely made sense' to 'seemed overwrought' (removes dissociative hint while keeping the self-doubt), and clarifies it's about emotional intensity rather than memory gaps.

issues.line_text: I checked my phone: 1:47 PM. The research had consumed me completelyΓÇöhours of work, though I couldn't swear I'd been in this chair the whole time.
issues.description: The phrase 'couldn't swear I'd been in this chair the whole time' hints at dissociative time loss. While Josh later rationalizes this as needing better breaks, the initial framing is too close to fugue-state symptoms in Act 1 (Chapter 7 is still early).
issues.fix: I checked my phone: 1:47 PM. The research had consumed me completelyΓÇöhours of work in what felt like minutes, the way deep focus always warped time.
issues.rationale: Reframes as normal hyperfocus (flow state) rather than memory gaps. This is safer for Act 1 while still showing Josh's obsessive work habits.

issues.line_text: Or maybe she was destroying evidence while I stood here mooning over her like an idiot.
issues.description: Josh jumping to 'destroying evidence' is premature. What evidence? At this point he suspects Eleanor of something vague but hasn't articulated a specific crime theory. This phrase implies he already believes she's guilty of something specific enough to have evidence.
issues.fix: Or maybe she was hiding something while I stood here mooning over her like an idiot.
issues.rationale: Changes 'destroying evidence' to 'hiding something'ΓÇökeeps Josh's suspicion without prematurely committing to a specific crime theory. More consistent with his still-forming doubts.

issues.line_text: The victim from four years ago. The only body ever recovered on the grounds.
issues.description: Lily died in February 2020, and the story takes place in November 2024. That's 4 years and 9 months, which rounds to 'nearly five years' more accurately than 'four years.' The article Josh reads should reflect when it was written (2020), not the current date.
issues.fix: The victim from 2020. The only body ever recovered on the grounds.
issues.rationale: Using the year (2020) is more precise and sidesteps the rounding issue. It's also how Josh would naturally reference itΓÇöby the case year, not elapsed time.

issues.line_text: When I tried it on, it fit loosely, the leather stiff from weather and time. The fingers were longer than mine, the palm wider. Someone bigger had worn this.
issues.description: Josh is 6'5" with broad shoulders and a muscular build per the Story Bible. Very few people would be 'bigger' than him with 'longer fingers' and a 'wider palm.' This description suggests the glove belonged to someone significantly larger, which is statistically unlikely and draws unnecessary attention.
issues.fix: When I tried it on, it fit roughlyΓÇöthe leather stiff from weather and time. Standard size large, common enough. Could belong to anyone.
issues.rationale: Removes the specific comparison to Josh's size (which would make the wearer exceptionally large) and reframes as generic/common. The glove is meant to be a red herring, not a clue, so making it non-distinctive serves the story better.

issues.line_text: I needed to be careful. Stay rational. Follow the evidence wherever it led.
issues.description: This closing thought positions Josh as the rational investigator following evidence. However, the chapter has shown him engaging in increasingly irrational behavior (watching Eleanor's cottage for hours, documenting her movements like surveillance, eavesdropping at 2 AM). The self-perception doesn't match his actions, which is good dramatic irony, but the final beat should hint at his lack of self-awareness rather than reinforce his self-image as rational.
issues.fix: I needed to be careful. Stay focused. Not let paranoia win.
issues.rationale: Changes 'Stay rational' to 'Stay focused' (less self-assured) and adds 'Not let paranoia win' (acknowledges the internal battle). This preserves Josh's unreliable narrator status while showing he's aware something is slipping, even if he can't name it.

notes: Overall the chapter does a good job maintaining Josh's unreliable narrator voice and his investigative obsession. The late-night documentation, the eavesdropping, and the surveillance behavior all read as concerning to readers while Josh rationalizes it as 'normal investigator behavior.' The glove at the cairn is appropriately treated as a red herring (Josh photographs the clearing but not the glove specifically). Eleanor's phone call ('running out of time') is ambiguous enough that readers will interpret it as sinister rather than terminal illness. The confrontation at the cairn where Eleanor tells Josh to 'leave this alone' reinforces reader perception that she's hiding guilt rather than grief. Strong misdirection overall with only minor technical issues to address.
